whatItDoes.text: The proposal would have asked voters in November 2026 to approve a half-cent sales tax to pay only for resurfacing, paving and widening local roads, collected for six years starting January 1, 2027. Because the motion failed 2 to 3 on May 5, 2026 (Amsler and Champion yes; Campbell, Allocco and Hawkins no), the roads tax is not on the ballot. Road work stays funded as before; the county memo says Hernando receives about $12 million a year in gas tax for resurfacing, signals, mowing, potholes and widening.

roads-surtax-rejected.note: Input had no date; the minutes show this vote at the May 5, 2026 Land Use Meeting (Legistar File 17419).

whatItDoes.text: Adds two new TheBus routes (Routes 10 and 11) and paratransit (ADA) service for them, raising the estimated yearly cost of the county's contract with operator RATP Dev USA from $3,443,250.04 to $5,200,328.16, plus a one-time $75,987 startup fee. For FY 2026 it is paid with federal transit grants (FTA 5311 and 5307), a state block grant, and a $947,829 local match moved from 9th-cent gas tax reserves; FY 2027 funding depends on future grants. The motion also put a discussion of bus routes on the first January 2027 agenda.

lg-56921.note: No later actions found yet; the January 2027 route discussion has not happened.

whatItDoes.text: Commits a $20,000 local government contribution, as a forgivable zero-interest loan deferred 20 years, to developer BG Hernando Owner 1 LP for "The Brook," a proposed 140-unit affordable apartment complex on about 6.9 acres on Rolling Rock Road near Brooksville for households at 35% to 60% of area median income. The money comes from federal HOME or state SHIP housing funds, and the form supports the developer's application to Florida Housing Finance Corporation for housing credits. The board added conditions of a 50-year affordability period and no tax abatement.

lg-57133.note: No record yet of whether Florida Housing Finance Corporation funded the project.

whatItDoes.text: Denied a request to rezone six platted lots on the north side of Eagle Nest Drive from R-1B residential to a planned single-family development that would have allowed up to six duplexes (12 homes) instead of six single-family homes. Because it was denied (Resolution No. 2026-157), the property stays vested for six single-family homes.

hernando-beach-duplex.note: Matched to Legistar File 17873 (REZ0000212026, Sept 1, 2026). Minutes for that meeting were not yet posted, so the 5 to 0 tally is from the input file.

whatItDoes.text: Rezoned land on the north side of Power Line Road from agricultural to Planned Development Project (Highway Commercial) with specific C-4 uses so a concrete batch plant can be built on about 5 acres in the interior of the property. The applicant said the plant would run Monday through Saturday, 7 a.m. to 6 p.m., and employ about 30 to 50 people. The board approved it with conditions (Resolution No. 2026-159).

concrete-plant.note: Matched to Legistar File 17856 (H2603). The 30-foot tree buffer named in the input was not confirmed; Sept 1, 2026 minutes were not yet posted.

whatItDoes.text: Gives up public right-of-way on portions of Nicasio Jay Court in Royal Highlands Unit 6, at the request of Hideaway Commercial, LLC, which said it wanted safer entry and exit from Royal Highlands. Utilities and county departments raised no objection, and staff reported no financial impact. The board adopted Resolution No. 2026-152, which is to be recorded in the county's public records.

The proposed ordinance would require owners of short-term vacation rentals in unincorporated Hernando County to register with the county, pass building and fire safety inspections, hold a state DBPR license, pay tourist development taxes, and not rent accessory structures as vacation rentals. The motion to deny it and not bring it back failed 2 to 2, so the ordinance was not rejected that day. Staff had asked for a majority-plus-one vote to advertise a second hearing for Sept 1, 2026.

lg-55779.note: Legistar shows no second public hearing on this ordinance as of Oct 27, 2026; July 28, 2026 minutes were not posted, so whether any other motion passed is unconfirmed.

whatItDoes.text: Ordinance No. 2026-15 stops the county from processing development orders and permits for data centers for up to 365 days unless extended or ended early. Staff said data centers use a lot of electricity and water and can be noisy, and that county rules did not address them. During the pause, planners are studying effects on water, wastewater, groundwater and the power grid, and plan to bring any needed Comprehensive Plan or zoning changes to the board.

datacenter-moratorium.note: Second hearing June 23, 2026 (Legistar File 17611); minutes list ayes Campbell, Amsler, Champion and Allocco.

whatItDoes.text: Would have bought a vacant 7,000-square-foot lot on Leonard Street (Brooksville Manor) from Antonio J. Cancelli-Patrick for $14,300 in federal CDBG money, with the stated intent of selling it to a nonprofit for affordable housing. Because the motion failed 2 to 2, the purchase did not happen that day.

afterward.text: At the same meeting the board voted 4 to 0 to bring the item back, with Commissioner Allocco asking how much a house would need to be built up to meet the flood zone.

The board approved the staff recommendation to buy the same lot for $14,300 in CDBG funds. The new memo describes the purchase as clearing blight, with any later affordable housing use needing HUD approval of a change of use.

whatItDoes.text: Hires Bandes Construction Company to build Fire Station No. 15 for $6,511,800, which includes a $250,000 owner's contingency. Bandes was the fourth-lowest of 11 bids; staff found two lower bids non-responsive and one non-responsible. The cost is split evenly between the fire and rescue funds ($3,255,900 each), and the county memo says it is a bond-funded project of up to $8 million, with reserves to be paid back once the debt is issued.

lg-54466.note: No construction start or finish date found in the county record.

whatItDoes.text: Pays Air Mechanical and Service Corporation $1,214,000 to replace the rooftop air conditioning units on the Bravo unit of the Hernando County Detention Center. It was the only bid received. The money comes from the Sheriff's Office related fund; $1.1 million was budgeted for FY 2026 and the other $114,000 comes from savings on the jail roof replacement project.

Rezones a parcel on the west side of Sunshine Grove Road, across from the Spring Ridge subdivision, from agricultural (with a special exception for a civic club) to Planned Development Project (Neighborhood Commercial) with specific C-1 commercial uses, and sets a master plan for it (Resolution No. 2026-047). The civic club special exception is eliminated. Staff reported no financial impact to the county.

Approves a revised master plan for the Seville West property on the north side of Kelso Street between Commercial Way and Downing Street (Resolution No. 2026-051). The site's plan had been locked in by a 2013 development agreement based on 2002 approvals; this vote replaces it with a new master plan and performance conditions. Staff reported no financial impact to the county.

lg-55353.note: The memo does not describe what the revision changes on the ground; the staff report attachment was not read.

whatItDoes.text: Changes the approved plan for property at the southeast corner of Alcan Avenue and Landover Boulevard so it allows mini-warehouses but no longer allows outdoor storage (Resolution No. 2026-028). Staff reported no financial impact to the county.

Rezones a 0.14-acre parcel on the south side of Cortez Boulevard, about 880 feet southeast of Mary's Fish Camp Road, to allow up to three vintage travel trailers as short-term vacation rentals, and allows boat rentals for all guests of Neptune's Old Florida Adventure Retreats (Resolution No. 2026-003). Staff reported no financial impact to the county.

Rezones a 0.49-acre lot bounded by Waterfall Drive and Eden Circle, shown as landscape area on the original Spring Hill master plan, so D.R. Horton can build one single-family home there (Resolution No. 2025-207). The Planning and Zoning Commission had voted 5 to 0 to recommend denial, citing compatibility and the applicant's absence. Staff reported no financial impact.

Hires Miles Partnership to market and advertise Hernando County tourism (Florida's Adventure Coast Visitors' Bureau) under a three-year contract estimated at $2,040,000, with two optional one-year renewals. It is paid with the 5% tourist bed tax, with $680,000 budgeted for the first year. Miles scored highest of 24 proposals.

This motion would have approved only part of the rezoning at the northeast corner of Commercial Way and Spring Hill Drive: lots three to five, with the southern U.S. 19 entrance removed and a sound barrier added, leaving lots one and two under their existing special-use zoning. Because it failed 2 to 3, no partial approval happened, and the board then denied the full request.

Denied Meridien Development's request to rezone the northeast corner of Commercial Way and Spring Hill Drive from special-use planned development to general commercial for a drive-in restaurant. The property keeps its existing zoning.

afterward.text: The board adopted Resolution No. 2025-204 ratifying the denial.
The developer filed a request for relief under the Florida Land Use and Environmental Dispute Resolution Act; county staff and the developer reached a mediated settlement on Jan. 27, 2026.
The board voted 3 to 2 to deny the mediated settlement agreement.
The board adopted Resolution No. 2026-070 ratifying the denial of the settlement.

whatItDoes.text: Gave the board's go-ahead, in concept, to borrow money through bonds for a list of capital projects, including a public safety training complex, a fire station, an animal shelter expansion, pier and bridge replacement, ball fields and county building work. The County Attorney said the vote was only about whether the board wants to move forward in concept. Staff said bond payments would come from sources such as impact fees, the EMS taxing unit (MSTU), the fire assessment (MSBU), tourist tax, tangible personal property tax and the general fund.

afterward.text: The board adopted Resolution No. 2026-053 authorizing 30-year Non-Ad Valorem Revenue Bonds, Series 2026, of up to $100 million for capital improvements.
The board amended the bond resolution (Resolution No. 2026-080) to add fleet replacement and a septic-to-sewer project, raising the limit to $112,500,000.
The Fire Station No. 15 contract memo describes that station as an approved bond-funded project of up to $8 million.

whatItDoes.text: Buys 924 Hale Avenue and an adjacent parcel near downtown Brooksville from Sundara Holdings for $1,963,000, to give the Clerk of Circuit Court and Comptroller more space. The money comes from public buildings impact fees (paid by new development), and the plan also uses $500,000 already budgeted in FY 2026 for a new constitutional officers building.

afterward.text: The purchase closed, with settlement charges bringing the total to $1,971,121.44.
The board approved a budget amendment moving the funding into the land acquisition account.
The board ratified a short-term license letting the existing tenant, Herbert Sherbert, Inc., stay up to 30 days (plus a possible 30-day extension) for $1,500 a month while it moved out.

whatItDoes.text: The ordinance would make parts of Mud River and the Weeki Wachee Gardens area year-round slow-speed boating zones to protect manatees. This motion would have rejected the ordinance and left the area as-is, with signs and public education instead. Because it failed 2 to 3, the ordinance was not rejected that day; it also was not adopted, and the board instead agreed to mail a survey to nearby residents and bring the results back.

afterward.text: The board voted not to do the resident survey, citing the cost to taxpayers, and to keep discussing educational signs with staff.

The board received the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission's reply that educational signs usually cannot be placed over or facing the water, and that it supports such signs at boat ramps, marinas and other upland access points.

lg-47439.note: No slow-speed zone ordinance has been adopted in the record found.

whatItDoes.text: Changed the yearly fire rescue assessment that appears on property tax bills for fiscal year 2026. The motion approved the increase at 5.75%, after a motion to cap it at 3% died for lack of a second. The final Resolution No. 2025-120 lists FY 2026 rates including $337.024 per home (shown against a current rate of $345.260), $85.805 per vacant parcel (from $19.357) and $0.202 per square foot of commercial space (from $0.182), plus a $25.36 base fee on every parcel (from $20.36), and limits future increases to 5.75% a year for five years.

afterward.text: The board ratified Resolution No. 2025-120 with the approved amounts, which were lower than the rates mailed in the public notice.

The board adopted Resolution No. 2026-116 setting new fire rescue assessment rates beginning in FY 2027, which also apply to City of Brooksville parcels after the two fire departments were consolidated.

whatItDoes.text: Ordinance No. 2025-03 adds rules to the county code on how unsolicited newspapers, flyers and circulars may be thrown onto private property, and lets residents opt out of receiving them. It regulates only the time, place and manner of delivery, not content. The county said the goal is to reduce litter and clogged storm drains.

Buys three parcels totaling about 16.9 acres just north of the Sheriff's Office headquarters at 18900 Cortez Boulevard from Bulk Transport Company East for $2,000,000, so the Sheriff's Office can expand. The money comes from general fund reserves through a budget amendment.

Settles a land use dispute with Raysor Ventures, whose request to rezone agricultural land for multifamily housing the board had denied 5 to 0 in June 2024. The settlement approves the rezoning (file H2427) with added conditions in the motion: a 90-unit limit, delivery of conservation land, no fence, a set bedroom mix and work with the county on a bus stop and sidewalk. Each side pays its own legal fees.

afterward.text: The board adopted Resolution No. 2025-061 to correct a scrivener's error in the settlement resolution.

whatItDoes.text: Declares a vacant 10,728-square-foot county lot on Kane Road in Spring Hill (valued at $39,666) surplus and gives it to the nonprofit You Thrive Florida to build an owner-occupied affordable home. The deed requires the land to stay affordable housing for 30 years and construction to be finished within 30 months, or the lot goes back to the county. State SHIP housing funds may help pay for construction once a building permit is approved.

The ordinance would have expanded the area of Hernando County where universal (mandatory) garbage collection applies. Because it failed 1 to 4, the district boundaries set in 2013 stay the same, and a companion resolution was not heard. The board then agreed to have staff prepare an item on a possible 2026 ballot referendum on expanding universal collection.

Changes the county code, which had required the county itself to run the animal shelter, so the commission can contract with an outside party to operate it (Ordinance No. 2024-18). Staff said the change was needed for a planned agreement with the Sheriff to run the shelter, with budget items to be transferred to the operator.

afterward.text: A later county memo states that the Sheriff's Office took over Animal Services operations in January 2025 under a memorandum of understanding.

lg-39811.note: Afterward date is January 2025 (exact day not given in the source).

whatItDoes.text: Ordinance No. 2026-02 puts a one-half cent sales tax on the Nov. 3, 2026 ballot to pay for the Hernando County Sheriff's Office's acquisition of law enforcement infrastructure, not operating costs. If voters approve, it would be collected from Jan. 1, 2027 through Dec. 31, 2031, and staff estimated about $14,454,126 in the first year. The board removed the original wording naming body-worn cameras before passing it 5 to 0.

afterward.text: The board received the state-required performance audit of programs that could receive the surtax, done by Mauldin & Jenkins for the Office of Program Policy Analysis and Government Accountability (OPPAGA).

sheriff-surtax.note: The referendum is Nov. 3, 2026; no result yet.

whatItDoes.text: Of the $850,000 the Sheriff's Office got for cybersecurity in FY 2024, $220,000 went unspent because vendors could not deliver by Sept. 30, 2024, and was returned to the county. This approval accepted the returned money and gave the $220,000 back to the Sheriff's Office in FY 2025 to finish the IT and cybersecurity upgrades.
